CausalChain: Chronic liver stress and oncogenic signaling -> Upregulation of m6A methyltransferases -> Aberrant m6A modification on tumor-suppressive lncRNAs -> Alteration in lncRNA secondary structure -> Impaired binding to epigenetic regulators (e.g., EZH2, DNMTs) -> Loss of repression on metabolic and proliferative oncogenic pathways -> Enhanced HCC progression
Hypothesis: Aberrant m6A modification of tumor-suppressive lncRNAs alters their secondary structure, impairing their interaction with epigenetic regulators and thus promoting metabolic reprogramming and cell proliferation in HCC; normalizing m6A levels on these lncRNAs can restore their tumor-suppressive functions and serve as a potential therapeutic strategy.
Abstract: Emerging evidence indicates that both epigenetic modifications and the intrinsic secondary structure of long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are critical determinants of their function. In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), dysregulated m6A modification patterns have been linked to altered stability and function of oncogenic and tumor-suppressive lncRNAs. We propose that aberrant m6A deposition on tumor-suppressive lncRNAs induces structural changes that weaken their binding to epigenetic regulators, thereby impairing their ability to repress key oncogenic pathways such as metabolic reprogramming and cell cycle progression. This study hypothesizes that restoring normal m6A levels will re-establish the proper secondary structure of these lncRNAs and reinstate their regulatory interactions, ultimately attenuating HCC progression. This novel insight may pave the way for therapeutics targeting lncRNA epitranscriptomic modifications in liver cancer.
